claim.why_it_matters: All five headings are flattened to H2, the same level the file uses for '## 8.4 References'. The clause hierarchy is destroyed on this page: 8.4.3.1.2 General format reads as a sibling of 8.4 rather than a great-grandchild, so any outline/TOC generated from the markdown mis-nests the identifier clauses. Sibling headings in the same run are levelled correctly elsewhere (e.g. '### 8.4.1 General', '#### 8.4.2.1 General'), so this is drift, not a house style.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on four independent grounds; no spec content differs.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING. Rendered E:/Temp/specrecon/v154/spec_p154.png at 300 dpi and read it directly. The printed page carries exactly five clause headings, and all five are present in ISO_COBOL.md verbatim, in order, with the correct dotted number and the correct title: '8.4.2.3.4 General rules' (line 6646), '8.4.3 Identifiers' (6659), '8.4.3.1 Identifier' (6662), '8.4.3.1.1 General' (6665), '8.4.3.1.2 General format' (6670). The claim's own quote of the markdown proves the text is there. The kind label 'missing-heading' is simply wrong -- not one heading is missing, misspelled, misnumbered, or reordered. Every body paragraph on the page (rule 8, rules 1)a-c and 2) of 8.4.2.3.4, the 8.4.3.1.1 sentence, Format 1/function-identifier-1, Format 2/qualified-data-name-with-subscripts-1) is likewise present and complete.

(2) THE PDF DOES NOT ENCODE THE LEVEL DISTINCTION THE CLAIM SAYS WAS LOST. Looking at the printed glyphs on p.154: '8.4.2.3.4  General rules', '8.4.3  Identifiers', '8.4.3.1  Identifier', '8.4.3.1.1  General' and '8.4.3.1.2  General format' are all set in the SAME bold serif, at the SAME point size, with the SAME left margin and the SAME vertical spacing. ISO does not step down type size by clause depth here. The PDF's depth signal is the dotted clause number itself -- and the markdown reproduces that number character-for-character. So the markdown loses nothing the source encoded; the '#' count is markdown-only presentation metadata with no counterpart in the PDF. This falls squarely under the 'formatting only' rejection criterion.

(3) THE CLAIM'S 'THIS IS DRIFT, NOT HOUSE STYLE' PREMISE IS INVERTED. Counted across the whole file: 162 four-deep clause headings (N.N.N.N) are at '##', versus only 24 at '####' or deeper. The flat-H2 rendering is the DOMINANT pattern at ~87%, not a page-154 anomaly. The two examples the claim cites as proof of correct levelling ('### 8.4.1 General', '#### 8.4.2.1 General') are the minority case. This is a global, mechanical artifact of the OCR/chunking pipeline (headings that open a page chunk emit '##'), uniform in kind across the document -- not a content defect localized to page 154.

(4) THE HEADING LEVELS ARE NOT A SEMANTIC HIERARCHY ANYWHERE IN THE FILE, SO NOTHING CAN BE 'DESTROYED' ON THIS PAGE. The running page header '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' appears 941 times at H1 -- including on this very page at line 6641 -- outranking every clause heading in the document. A naive outline built from '#' depth is already meaningless file-wide; page 154 neither improves nor worsens that. Meanwhile the true hierarchy is fully machine-recoverable two ways: from the dotted number, and from the anchors that precede each heading (<a id="section-8-4-3">, <a id="section-8-4-3-1">, <a id="section-8-4-3-1-1">, <a id="section-8-4-3-1-2">), all of which are present and correctly derived.

Net: zero characters of normative spec text differ between the PDF and the transcription on page 154. Not a reconciliation finding. At most it is a cosmetic, document-wide markdown-styling inconsistency, and if it is ever addressed it must be addressed as a single global pass over all 162 sites (derive the heading level from the dot-count of the clause number, and demote the 941 running headers off H1), never as a page-154 edit.
verdict.corrected_description: No discrepancy. All five headings (8.4.2.3.4 General rules, 8.4.3 Identifiers, 8.4.3.1 Identifier, 8.4.3.1.1 General, 8.4.3.1.2 General format) are present in the markdown with correct numbers and titles, and the PDF prints all five in identical typography -- the print encodes depth only via the dotted clause number, which the transcription preserves exactly. The reported issue is markdown '#'-level styling, which has no PDF counterpart, and the flat-H2 rendering is the file's dominant pattern (162 of 186 four-deep headings), not page-154 drift. The file's heading levels are not a hierarchy at all: the running header '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' sits at H1 on 941 pages, including this one.
